desc:
A base b ≥ 2 is good for n if the representation of n in base b consists only of the digit 1 (at least two digits long), i.e. n = 1 + b + b2 + ... + bm-1 for some m ≥ 2.

Return the smallest good base of n. A good base always exists, because n - 1 works: n = 1 + (n - 1).

Examples: 13 gives 3 (13 is 111 in base 3); 4681 gives 8 (11111 in base 8); 3 gives 2 (11 in base 2).
hints: Trying every base from 2 up to n - 1 is far too slow. Think about the other unknown: the number of digits m. How large can it be?
A smaller base means more digits, and since b ≥ 2 we have n ≥ 2m - 1, so m ≤ 31. Iterate m from the largest possible value downward; the first m that has a valid base gives the smallest base.

For a fixed m, the sum 1 + b + ... + bm-1 is strictly increasing in b, so at most one base fits. Binary search the largest b in [2, sqrt(n)] whose sum is at most n and check whether the sum equals n. If no m ≥ 3 works, return n - 1.
editorial: Switch the viewpoint from the base to the digit count. For each length m, the value S(b) = 1 + b + ... + bm-1 is strictly increasing in b, so there is at most one base b with S(b) = n, and it can be found by binary search on b comparing S(b) with n. Because the base shrinks as the length grows, scanning m from large to small and returning the first success yields the smallest base.

Bounds: b = 2 needs n ≥ 2m - 1, so m is at most the bit length of n, i.e. at most 31 here. For m ≥ 3 we have b2 < n, so the base is at most sqrt(n) (about 46,341). Length m = 2 always succeeds with b = n - 1 and acts as the fallback. The total work is about 30 lengths times 16 binary-search steps times an O(m) evaluation of the geometric sum, which is trivial.
